cues.en: All right, good afternoon. Today's speaker is Peter Thiel. Peter was the founder of PayPal and Palantir and Founders Fund and has invested in most of the tech companies in Silicon Valley. And he's going to talk about strategy and competition. Thank you for coming, Peter. Awesome, thanks. Sam, thanks for inviting me. Thanks for having me. I sort of have a, I have a single e-day speaks that I'm completely obsessed with in
cues.zh: 好的，下午好。今天的演讲嘉宾是 Peter Thiel。Peter 是 PayPal、Palantir 和 Founders Fund 的创始人，投资过硅谷绝大多数科技公司。今天他要分享的是战略与竞争。谢谢你的到来，Peter。太棒了，谢谢。Sam，感谢你的邀请，感谢大家。在商业方面，我一直有一个深深着迷的执念，

cues.en: on the business side which is that if you're starting a company, if you're the founder, entrepreneur starting a company, you always want to aim for monopoly. And you want to always avoid competition. And so, hence competition is for losers, something we'll be talking about today. I'd like to start by saying something about the basic idea of when you start one of these companies,
cues.zh: 那就是如果你要创业，作为创始人或创业者，你永远应该追求垄断，永远要避开竞争。所以才说“竞争是留给失败者的”，这也是我们今天要聊的主题。我想先谈谈创立这类公司时的一个基本逻辑：

cues.en: how you go about creating value. And there's this question, what makes a business valuable? And I wanna suggest that there's basically a very simple formula that you have a valuable company, two things are true. Number one, that it creates X dollars of value for the world. And number two, that you capture Y percent of X. And the critical thing that I think people,
cues.zh: 你该如何创造价值。这里有个问题：什么决定了一家公司的价值？我认为有一个非常简单的公式，一家有价值的公司必须满足两点：第一，它为世界创造了价值 X；第二，你能捕获其中 Y% 的价值。而我认为大家

cues.en: always miss in the sort of analysis is that x and y are completely independent variables. And so x can be very big, y can be very small, x can be of intermediate size, and if y is reasonably big, you can still get a very big business. So to create a valuable company, you have to basically both create something of value and capture some fraction of the value of what you've created. And sort of just to.
cues.zh: 在这类分析中往往会忽略的关键在于：X 和 Y 是完全独立的变量。所以 X 可以非常大，而 Y 非常小；或者 X 处于中等规模，但只要 Y 足够大，你依然能做成一家极其庞大的企业。因此，要打造一家有价值的公司，你既要创造出有价值的东西，又要从中捕获一部分价值。为了

cues.en: Just to illustrate this as a contrast, if you sort of compare the US airline industry with a company like Google on search, if you sort of measure by the size of these industries, you could say that airlines are still more important than search. If you just measure it, say, by revenues, there's $195 billion in domestic revenues in 2012.
cues.zh: 直观说明这种对比，我们可以把美国航空业和 Google 的搜索业务做个比较。如果单纯按行业规模来衡量，你可能会觉得航空业依然比搜索更重要。如果按营收来看，2012 年美国国内航空业收入有 1950 亿美元，

cues.en: Google had just north of 50 billion. And certainly, on some intuitive level, if you were given a choice and said, well, do you want to get rid of all air travel, or do you want to get rid of your ability to use search engines, the intuition would be that air travel is something that's more important than search. And this is, of course, just the domestic numbers. If you'd looked at this globally, airlines are much, much bigger than searcher than Google is.
cues.zh: 而 Google 当时刚刚突破 500 亿。从直觉上讲，如果给你一个选择：是彻底放弃所有空中航行，还是放弃使用搜索引擎，直觉都会告诉你航空出行比搜索更重要。当然，这还仅仅是美国本土的数据，放眼全球，航空业的规模更是远超搜索业务和 Google。

cues.en: But the profit margins are quite a bit less. They were marginally profitable in 2012. I think the entire 100 year history of the airline industry, the cumulative profits in the US have been approximately zero. The companies make money, they episodically go bankrupt, they get recapitalized, and you sort of cycle and repeat. And this is reflected in the combined market capitalization of the airline industries, maybe something.
cues.zh: 但航空业的利润率要低得多。2012 年他们只是勉强盈利。纵观航空业整整百年的历史，美国航空业的累计利润几乎为零。这些公司赚点钱，然后周期性破产，进行资本重组，如此循环往复。这种状况也反映在整个航空业的总市值上，大概……

cues.en: of the US airline industry, something like a quarter that of Google. So you have a search engine, much, much smaller than air travel, but much more valuable. And I think this reflects these very different valuations on X and Y. So if we look at perfect competition, there's some pros and cons to the world of perfect competition. On a high level,
cues.zh: 美国航空业的……大约相当于 Google 的四分之一。所以，搜索引擎的规模比航空旅行小得多得多，但价值却高得多。我认为这反映了 X 和 Y 上截然不同的估值。那么看完全竞争，完全竞争的世界有优点也有缺点。从宏观层面看，

cues.en: It's always, this is what you study in Econ 1. It's easy to model, which I think is why Econ professors like talking about perfect competition. It somehow is efficient, especially in a world where things are static, because you have all the consumer surplus gets captured by everybody. And politically, it's what we're told is good in our society, that you want to have competition, and this is somehow a good thing. Of course, there are a lot of negatives. It's generally not that good if you're,
cues.zh: 这个嘛，这是经济学入门课的内容。它容易建模，我觉得这就是经济学教授喜欢谈完全竞争的原因。它不知为何是有效率的，尤其在静态世界里，因为所有消费者剩余都被所有人获取了。政治上，社会告诉我们竞争是好的，这不知怎么就是好事。当然，有很多负面。一般来说，如果你……

cues.en: You're involved in anything that's hyper competitive because you often don't make money. I'll come back to this a little bit later. So I think at one end of the spectrum, you have industries that are perfectly competitive. And at the other end of the spectrum, you have things that I would say are monopolies. And they're much stable longer term businesses. You have more capital.
cues.zh: 参与任何竞争极其激烈的事情，这通常不太好，因为常常赚不到钱。稍后我会再谈这一点。所以我认为，光谱一端是完全竞争的行业。另一端是我所说的垄断。它们是更稳定的长期生意。你有更多资本。

cues.en: And if you get a creative monopoly for inventing something new, I think it's symptomatic of having created something really valuable. And so I do think the sort of the extreme binary view of the world I always articulate is that there are exactly two kinds of businesses in this world. There are businesses that are perfectly competitive and there are businesses that are monopolies. And there's shockingly little that is in between.
cues.zh: 如果你因发明新东西而获得创造性垄断，我认为这标志着创造了真正有价值的东西。所以我确实认为，我常说的那种极端二元世界观是：世界上恰好有两类企业。完全竞争的企业和垄断企业。中间地带少得惊人。

cues.en: And this dichotomy is not understood very well because people are constantly lying about the nature of the businesses they're in. And this is why, this is, in my mind, this is the most important, it's not necessarily the most important thing in business, but I think it's the most important business idea that people don't understand, that there are just these two kinds of businesses. And so let me say a little bit about the lies that people tell. And so you basically, the basic, if you sort of imagine that there was a spectrum.
cues.zh: 这种二分法没有被很好理解，因为人们总在谎报自己所在企业的性质。这就是为什么，在我看来，这是最重要的——不一定是商业中最重要的事，但我认为这是人们没理解的最重要商业理念：只有这两类企业。让我稍微谈谈人们说的谎。基本上，如果你想象有一个光谱，

cues.en: of companies from perfect competition to monopoly. The apparent differences are quite small because the people who have monopolies pretend not to. They will basically say, and it's because you don't want to get regulated by the government, you don't want the government to come after you. So you will never say that you have a monopoly. So anyone who has a monopoly will pretend that they're in incredible competition. And on the other end of the spectrum, if you are incredibly competitive,
cues.zh: 这个光谱涵盖从完全竞争到垄断的企业。表面差异很小，因为拥有垄断的人假装没有。他们基本上会说，这是因为你不想被政府监管，不想政府找你麻烦。所以你永远不会说自己有垄断。所以任何有垄断的人都会假装自己处于极其激烈的竞争中。而在光谱另一端，如果你竞争极其激烈，

cues.en: And if you're in some sort of business where you will never make any money, you will be tempted to tell a lie that goes in the other direction where you will say that you're doing something unique that is somehow less competitive than it looks. Because you will want to differentiate, you'll want to try to track capital or something like that. So if the monopolists pretend not to have monopolies, the non-monopolists pretend to have monopolies, the apparent difference is very small.
cues.zh: 如果你处在某种永远赚不到钱的生意里，你会忍不住往另一个方向撒谎，说自己在做某种独特的事，竞争没有看起来那么激烈。因为你想差异化，想吸引资本之类。所以，垄断者假装没有垄断，非垄断者假装有垄断，表面差异就非常小。

cues.en: Whereas the real difference, I would submit, is actually quite big. And so there's this distortion that happens because of the lies people tell about their businesses. And the lies are sort of in these opposite directions. Let me drill a little bit down further on the way these lies work. And so the basic lie you tell as a-
cues.zh: 但依我看来，真正的差距其实非常大。正因为人们对自家业务说的那些谎话，才导致了这种扭曲。而且这些谎言是朝截然相反的两个方向发展的。让我进一步深入讲讲这些谎言是如何起作用的。那么，作为非垄断企业，你说的最基本谎言就是——

cues.en: non-monopoly is that we're in a very small market. The basic lie you tell the monopoly is that the market you're in is much bigger than it looks. And so typically, if you want to think of this in sort of set theoretic terms, you could say that a monopoly tells a lie where you describe your business as the union of these vastly different markets. And the non-monopolist describes it as the intersection. So that
cues.zh: 非垄断企业会说“我们身处一个极小的市场”。而垄断企业说的基本谎言则是“我们所在的市场比看起来要大得多”。通常，如果用集合论的视角来看，垄断者撒谎时，会把业务描述为多个截然不同的市场的“并集”；而非垄断者则会将其描述为“交集”。这样一来，

cues.en: In effect, if you're a non-monopolist, you will rhetorically describe your market as super small. You're the only person in that market. If you have monopoly, you will describe it as super big and there's lots of competition in it. So some examples of how this works in practice. So I always use restaurants as the example of a terrible business. And this is always sort of my ideas. Capitalism and competition are antonyms.
cues.zh: 实际上，如果你是非垄断企业，你在话术上就会把市场描述得极其狭小，小到只有你一家。如果你拥有垄断地位，就会把它描述得极其庞大，且竞争异常激烈。举几个实际例子来说明。我总喜欢拿餐馆来当糟糕生意的典型代表。这也契合我一贯的观点：资本主义和竞争其实是反义词。

cues.en: Capital is someone who accumulates capital. World of perfect competition is a world where all the capital gets competed away. So you're opening a restaurant business. No one wants to invest because you just lose money. So you have to tell some idiosyncratic narrative and you'll say something like, well we're the only British food restaurant in Palo Alto. So it's British, Palo Alto, and of course that's too small a market because people may be able to drive all the way to Mountain View or even Menlo Park. And there probably are.
cues.zh: 资本家是积累资本的人，而完全竞争的世界，是一个所有资本都在竞争中被消耗殆尽的世界。比如你要开一家餐馆，没人愿意投资，因为只会亏钱。所以你必须讲一套奇特的话术，比如你会说：“我们是 Palo Alto 唯一一家英式餐厅。”也就是“英国菜”交上“Palo Alto”，这当然是个狭窄过头的市场，因为人们完全可以开车去 Mountain View 甚至 Menlo Park。而且世界上很可能

cues.en: no people who eat nothing but British food, at least no people who are still alive. And so that's sort of a fictitiously narrow market. There's sort of a Hollywood version of this where the way movies always get pitched is, okay, it's like a college football star joins an elite group of hackers to catch the shark that killed his friend.
cues.zh: 根本没有人只吃英国菜——至少活人里没有。所以这纯粹是一个虚构出来的狭窄市场。好莱坞也有类似的翻版，电影路演提案总是这种套路：“一个大学橄榄球明星加入了一个顶尖黑客组织，去抓咬死他朋友的那条鲨鱼。”

cues.en: Sorry. And so that's, now that is a movie that has not yet been made. But, but, but the question is, is, is that the right category or is the correct category, it's just another movie. In which case, you know, there are lots of those. It's super competitive, incredibly hard to make money. No one ever makes money in Hollywood doing movies. It's, it's really, really hard. And so you always have this question about does the intersection.
cues.zh: 抱歉。这种电影目前确实还没人拍过。但问题在于，这真的算一个正确的品类吗？还是说更准确的归类只是“又一部普通电影”？要是这样的话，同类电影就太多了。竞争极其激烈，赚钱难如登天。好莱坞拍电影基本没人能赚到钱，实在太难了。所以你总要追问：这种交集……

cues.en: Is it real? Does it make sense? Does it have value that one should ask? And of course, there are startup versions of this where you, and the sort of really bad versions, you just take a whole series of buzzwords, sharing mobile social apps. You combine them and you have some kind of narrative. And whether or not that's a real business or not is generally a bad sign. So it's almost this pattern recognition when you have this rhetoric of this sort of intersections.
cues.zh: 它真的存在吗？合乎逻辑吗？有价值吗？这些都是该问的问题。当然，创业圈也有类似版本，尤其是那些非常糟糕的案例，就是拼凑一堆流行词：“共享”、“移动”、“社交应用”。把它们组合在一起拼出一个故事。这种东西到底算不算真正的业务，通常都是个坏兆头。所以只要听到这种拿“交集”包装出来的说辞，你几乎就能一眼识别出这种套路。

cues.en: It generally does not work. The something of somewhere is really mostly just the nothing of nowhere. It's like the Stanford of North Dakota. One of a kind, but it's not Stanford. So let's look at the opposite. The opposite lie is if you are, let's say, the search company that's down the street from here and has about a happy 66% market share.
cues.zh: 这通常行不通。“某地的某某”大多只是噱头，根本微不足道。就像“北达科他州的 Stanford”，虽说独一无二，但它终究不是 Stanford。那我们来看看反面的情况。反向的谎言是，假设你是街角那家日子过得挺滋润、拥有 66% 市场份额的搜索公司，

cues.en: and is completely dominant in the search market. Google has almost never described itself as a search engine these days. And instead, it describes itself in all these different ways. So it sometimes says it's an advertising company. So if it was searched, you'd say, wow, it's like.
cues.zh: 在搜索市场占据绝对统治地位。如今 Google 几乎从不称自己是搜索引擎。相反，它换着各种花样来描述自己。它有时会说自己是一家广告公司。因为如果说是搜索，大家就会觉得：哇，这简直……

cues.en: It has this huge market share that's really, really crazy. It's like an incredible monopoly. It's much more robust monopoly than Microsoft ever had in the 90s. Maybe that's why it's making so much money. But if you say it's an advertising market, you could say, well, search advertising is 17 billion. And that's part of online advertising, which is much bigger. And then all US advertising is bigger.
cues.zh: 市场份额大得惊人，这简直是不可思议的垄断。这比 Microsoft 在 90 年代的垄断还要稳固得多。也许这就是它这么能赚钱的原因。但如果你说是广告市场，你就可以说：搜索广告只有 170 亿，它只是规模大得多的线上广告的一部分，而全美广告市场就更大了。

cues.en: And then by the time you get to global advertising, that's close to 500 billion. And so you're talking about three and a half percent. So a tiny part of this much larger market. Or if you don't want to be an advertising company, you can always say that you're a technology company. And so, sorry, let me see. And so the, and, and so.
cues.zh: 再放到全球广告来看，那就是近 5000 亿的规模。这样看你只占了 3.5%，在这个庞大市场里不过是沧海一粟。或者你不想自称广告公司，你随时可以说自己是一家科技公司。抱歉，让我想想，所以……

cues.en: And the technology market is something like a $1 trillion market. And the narrative that you tell is Google and the technology market is, well, we're competing with all the car companies with our self-driving cars. We're competing with Apple on TVs and iPhones.
cues.zh: 整个科技市场差不多有 1 万亿美元规模。你给 Google 编织的故事就变成了：我们在科技市场里，正用自动驾驶汽车与各大车企竞争，在电视和手机上与 Apple 竞争。

cues.en: We're competing with Facebook, we're competing with Microsoft on office products, we're competing with Amazon on cloud services. And so we are in this giant technology market where there's competition in every direction you look. And no, we're not the monopoly the government's looking for, and we should not get regulated in any way whatsoever. And so I think one has to always be super aware that there are these very powerful incentives.
cues.zh: 我们在与 Facebook 竞争，在办公软件上与 Microsoft 竞争，在云服务上与 Amazon 竞争。我们身处这个庞大的科技市场，四面八方都是竞争。不，我们才不是政府要找的垄断者，我们根本不该受到任何监管。所以我觉得，大家必须时刻看清，背后有一股强大的动力，

cues.en: to distort the nature of these markets one way or the other. So the evidence of narrow markets in the tech industry is if you basically just, if you look at sort of the, some of the big tech companies, Apple, Google, Microsoft, Amazon, they've just been building up cash for year after year and you have these incredibly high profit margins.
cues.zh: 在从各个角度扭曲这些市场的真实面貌。科技行业实际上是狭小垄断市场的证据在于，如果你看看 Apple、Google、Microsoft、Amazon 这些科技巨头，它们年复一年地积累巨额现金，利润率高得惊人。

cues.en: I would say that one of the reasons the tech industry in the US has been so successful financially is because it's prone to creating all these monopoly-like businesses. And it's reflected by the fact that these companies just accumulate so much cash, they don't even know what to do with it beyond a certain point. So let me say a few things about-
cues.zh: 我认为美国科技行业在商业上如此成功的原因之一，就是它极易催生这种类似垄断的企业。这正反映在它们囤积了如此庞大的现金储备，到后来甚至不知道拿这些钱做什么。接下来我想谈几点……

cues.en: about how to build a monopoly. And I think one of the sort of very counterintuitive ideas that comes out of this monopoly thread is that you want to go after small markets. If you're a startup, you want to get to a monopoly. You're starting a new company, you want to get to a monopoly. Monopolies, you have a large share of a market.
cues.zh: 关于如何建立垄断。顺着这个垄断逻辑，会得出一条非常反直觉的观点：你应该瞄准小市场。初创公司的目标是形成垄断；创办新公司，你想达成垄断。而垄断，意味着你占据了极大的市场份额。

cues.en: How do you get to a large share of a market? You start with a really small market and you take over that whole market. And then over time, you find ways to expand that market in concentric circles. And the thing that's always a big mistake is going after a giant market on day one.
cues.zh: 怎样才能拿到巨大的市场份额？从一个极小的市场做起，彻底拿下它。随着时间推移，再想办法像同心圆一样逐步向外扩张。而最常犯的重大错误，就是第一天就去追逐一个庞大的市场。

cues.en: Because that's typically evidence that you somehow haven't defined the categories correctly. And it normally means that there's going to be too much competition in one way or another. And so I think almost all the successful companies in Silicon Valley had some model of starting with small markets and expanding. And if you take Amazon, you start with just a bookstore.
cues.zh: 因为这通常说明你对品类的定义还不够准确。而且往往意味着你必然会面临过度激烈的竞争。所以我认为硅谷几乎所有成功的公司，其模式都是从小市场起步并逐步扩张。以 Amazon 为例，最初不过是一家书店。

cues.en: We have all the books in the world, so it's a better bookstore than anybody else has in the world when it starts in the 90s. It's online, there's things you can do you can't do before. And then you gradually expand into all sorts of different forms of e-commerce and other things beyond that. eBay, you start with PES dispensers, you move on to Beanie Babies, and eventually it's all these different auctions for all these sorts of different goods.
cues.zh: 我们拥有世界上所有的图书，所以 90 年代刚起步时，它就比世界上任何一家实体书店都更好。它在线上，能做到以前做不到的事。然后你再逐步扩展到各种不同形态的电商以及更广阔的领域。拿 eBay 来说，从 PES 糖果盒起步，再到 Beanie Babies 玩偶，最终演变成各类不同商品的拍卖平台。

cues.en: And what's very counterintuitive about many of these companies is they often start with markets that are so small that people don't think that they're valuable at all when you get started. The PayPal version of this was, we started with power sellers on eBay, which was about 20,000 people.
cues.zh: 这些公司很反直觉的一点在于，它们切入的市场往往小到让大家觉得一开始根本毫无价值。PayPal 的版本是，我们起步于 eBay 上的超级卖家，一共也就大约两万人。

cues.en: When we first saw this happening in December of 99, January 2000, right after we launched, there was a sense that these were all, it was such a small market, it was terrible. We thought these were terrible customers to have. It's just people selling junk on the Internet. Why in the world do we want to be going after this market? But there was a way to get a product that was much better for everybody in that market. You could, and we got to something like 25, 30% market penetration in two or three months.
cues.zh: 1999 年 12 月、2000 年 1 月产品刚上线时，我们第一次看到这种情况，感觉这市场太小了，简直糟糕透顶。我们觉得这帮客户太差劲了，不过是一帮在网上卖破烂的人，我们到底为什么要盯上这个市场？但其实有办法做出一款对该市场中的所有人来说都好得多的产品。我们做到了，在两三个月内就拿下了大约 25% 到 30% 的市场渗透率。

cues.en: And you got some walk-in, you got brand recognition, and you're able to build the business from there. So I always think these very small markets are quite underrated. The Facebook version of this I always give is that the initial market at Facebook was 10,000 people at Harvard. It went from 0% to 60% market share in 10 days. That was a very auspicious start. The way this gets analyzed in business schools is always,
cues.zh: 你有了客流，有了品牌知名度，就能以此为基础把业务做大。所以我总觉得这些极小的市场被严重低估了。我常拿 Facebook 举例，它最初的市场就是哈佛的 1 万名学生。它在 10 天内市场份额就从 0% 冲到了 60%。那是一个非常完美的开端。但在商学院里，人们对此的分析总是：

cues.en: That's ridiculous. It's such a small market. It can't have any value at all. And so I think the business school analysis of Facebook early on or of PayPal early on or of eBay early on is that the markets were perhaps so small as to have almost no value. And they would have had little value had they stayed small, but it turned out there were ways to then grow them concentrically. And that's what made them so valuable. Now I think the opposite
cues.zh: “太荒谬了。市场这么小，根本不可能有任何价值。”所以商学院早期对 Facebook、PayPal 或 eBay 的分析，往往认为这些市场小到几乎毫无价值。如果它们一直局限于小规模，确实没什么价值，但事实证明，后续完全有办法以同心圆的方式向外扩张。正是这一点让它们变得极具价值。而我认为相反的

cues.en: version of this is always where you have super big markets. And there's so many different things that went wrong with all the clean tech companies in the last decade. But one theme that ran through almost all of them was they all started with massive markets. And every clean tech PowerPoint presentation that one saw in the years 2005 to 2008, which was sort of the clean tech bubble in Silicon Valley, started with we're in the energy market.
cues.zh: 典型，则是那些一上来就瞄准超大市场的情况。过去十年里，那些清洁技术公司出问题的原因五花八门。但贯穿几乎所有公司的一个共同点，就是它们都从极其庞大的市场切入。在 2005 到 2008 年间——也就是硅谷清洁技术泡沫时期——你能看到的每一份清洁技术 PowerPoint 演示，开头都是“我们做的是能源市场”。

cues.en: We're in a market that's measured in hundreds of billions or trillions of dollars. And then once you're sort of a minnow in a vast ocean, that's not a good place to be. That means that you have tons of competitors and you don't even know who all the competitors are. And so you want to be a one of a kind company where it's the only one.
cues.zh: 我们身处一个规模数千亿乃至数万亿美元的市场。但如果你成了汪洋中的一条小鱼，处境就很不妙了。这意味着你有大量的竞争对手，甚至都不知道他们全是谁。因此，你想成为一家独一无二、无可替代的公司。

cues.en: In a small ecosystem, you don't want to be the fourth online pet food company. You don't want to be the 10th thin film solar panel company. You don't want to be the 100th restaurant in Palo Alto. Your restaurant industry is a trillion dollar industry. So if you do a market size analysis, you conclude restaurants are a fantastic business to go into. And it's often large markets, large existing markets typically mean that you have tons of competition, very, very hard to differentiate. So the first very counterintuitive
cues.zh: 在小生态里，你不想做第四家在线宠物食品公司，不想做第十家薄膜太阳能板公司，也不想做 Palo Alto 的第 100 家餐馆。餐饮业是个万亿美元级的大产业。如果做市场规模分析，你会得出开餐馆是个极好生意的结论。但这种庞大的现有市场通常意味着竞争极度激烈，非常难做出差异化。所以第一个非常反直觉的……

cues.en: idea is to go after small markets, often markets that are so small people don't even notice them, they don't think that they make sense. That's where you get a foothold. And then if those markets are able to expand, you can scale into a big monopoly business. There's sort of several different characteristics of these monopoly businesses that I like to.
cues.zh: 想法就是瞄准小市场，往往小到别人根本注意不到、觉得做这个没意义。但那正是你能立足的地方。如果这些市场能扩张，你就能做大规模，成为庞大的垄断企业。关于这些垄断企业，我想重点谈……

cues.en: focus on and there's probably no sort of single formula to it. And I always think that in technology, there's always a sense that the history of technology is such that every moment happens only once. And so the next Mark Zuckerberg won't build a social network. The next Larry Page won't be building a search engine. The next Bill Gates won't be building an operating system. And if you're copying these people, you're not learning from them. And so there is always.
cues.zh: 几点特征，虽然可能并没有什么万能公式。我总觉得在科技界，科技的发展历史表明，每个时刻都只发生一次。下一个 Mark Zuckerberg 不会去做社交网络，下一个 Larry Page 不会去做搜索引擎，下一个 Bill Gates 也不会去做操作系统。如果你在抄袭他们，你就没学到精髓。因此总会有……

cues.en: these very unique businesses that are doing something that's not been done before end up having the potential to be a monopoly. The opening line in Anna Karenina is that all happy families are alike, all unhappy families are unhappy in their own special way. And the opposite is true in business where I think all happy companies are different because they're doing something very unique.
cues.zh: 这些做着前所未有之事的独特企业，最终才具备成为垄断者的潜力。《安娜·卡列尼娜》的开篇是：幸福的家庭都是相似的，不幸的家庭各有各的不幸。而在商业世界里恰恰相反，我认为所有幸福的公司都是不同的，因为它们做的事情非常独特。

cues.en: all unhappy companies are alike because they fail to escape the essential sameness that is competition. And so one sort of characteristic of a monopoly technology company is some sort of proprietary technology. My sort of crazy, somewhat arbitrary rule of thumb is you want to have a technology that's an order of magnitude better than the next best thing.
cues.zh: 而不幸的公司都是相似的，因为它们无法摆脱竞争带来的同质化本质。所以垄断型科技公司的一个特征，就是拥有某种专有技术。我有一个有点疯狂、稍显武断的经验法则：你的技术必须比第二好的替代品好上一个数量级。

cues.en: So Amazon had over ten times as many books, maybe not that high tech, but you figure out a way to sell ten times as many books in an efficient online way. PayPal, the alternative for PayPal was using checks to send money on eBay, took seven to ten days to clear. PayPal could do it more than ten times as fast. So you want to have some sort of very, very powerful improvement in some order, maybe an order of magnitude improvement on some.
cues.zh: 比如 Amazon 当时的图书品类是对手的十倍以上，这也许不算高深技术，但他们找到了在网上高效售卖十倍图书的方法。PayPal 也是如此，在 eBay 上的替代方案是用支票付款，需要 7 到 10 天才能结清，而 PayPal 能够快十倍以上。所以你必须具备某种极其强大的提升，在某些维度上带来数量级式的飞跃。

cues.en: key dimension. Of course, if you actually come with something totally new, it's just like an infinite improvement. So I would say the iPhone was the first smartphone that worked. And so that's maybe not infinite, but it's sort of definitely an order of magnitude or more of an improvement. So I think the technology is designed to give you a massive delta over the next best thing.
cues.zh: 关键维度。当然，如果你真拿出了全新的东西，那就好比是无限大的提升。可以说 iPhone 是第一款真正好用的智能手机。这或许不算无限大，但绝对带来了一个数量级以上的提升。因此我认为，技术生来就是要拉开与次优方案之间的巨大代差。

cues.en: I think there often are network effects that can kick in that really help. These lead to monopolies over time. The thing that's very tricky about network effects is they're often very hard to get started. And so even though everyone understands how valuable they are, there's always this incredibly tricky question, why is it valuable to the first person who's doing something? Economies of scale, if you have something with very high fixed costs.
cues.zh: 我认为网络效应往往会发挥关键作用并大有助益。长此以往就会走向垄断。网络效应最棘手的地方在于极难启动。所以尽管大家都知道它有多大价值，却总要面对这个极难回答的问题：对于第一个使用者来说，它到底有什么价值？至于规模经济，如果你的固定成本极高，

cues.en: Very low marginal costs. That's typically a monopoly-like business. And then there's this thing of branding, which is sort of like just this idea that gets lodged in people's brains. I never quite understand how branding works. So I never invest in companies where it's just about branding. But it is, I think, a real phenomenon that creates real value. I think one of the things, I'm going to come back to this a little bit towards the end. But one of the things that's very striking
cues.zh: 边际成本极低，那就是典型的类垄断业务。此外还有品牌，它就像是深植于人们脑海中的观念。我从来没太搞懂品牌的运作机制，所以我从不投资纯靠品牌的公司。但我认为这确实是一种能创造真实价值的客观现象。有一点我快结束时还会提到，但非常引人注目的是，

cues.en: is that software businesses are often, are for some reason very good at some of these things. They're especially good at the economies of scale part, because the marginal cost of software is zero. And so if you get something that works in software, it's often significantly better than the existing solution. And then you have these tremendous economies of scale, and you can scale fairly quickly. So even if the market starts small, you can grow your business quickly enough to
cues.zh: 软件业务不知为何往往非常擅长其中一些方面。它们尤其擅长发挥规模经济效应，因为软件的边际成本为零。因此如果你在软件上做出了切实可行的方案，往往会显著优于现有方案。随之而来的便是巨大的规模效应，而且扩张极快。所以即便起步市场很小，你的业务增长也足够快，足以

cues.en: stay at the same size as the growing market and maintain the sort of monopoly power. Now, the critical thing about these monopolies is it's not enough to have a monopoly for just a moment. The critical thing is to have one that lasts over time. And so, you know, the Silicon Valley is always the sort of idea that you want to be the first mover. And I always think it's, in some ways,
cues.zh: 跟上不断扩大的市场规模，并维持这种垄断地位。谈到这些垄断，最关键的一点在于：只垄断一时是不够的。最关键的是要能长久维持。所以你看，Silicon Valley 总是充斥着这种想法，觉得必须抢做先发者。而我始终认为，在某种程度上，

cues.en: The better framing is you want to be the last mover. You want to be the last company in a category. Those are the ones that are really valuable. Microsoft was the last operating system, at least for many decades. Google is the last search engine. Facebook will be valuable if it turns out to be the last social networking site. And one way to think of this last mover value is this idea that most of the value in these companies exists far in the future.
cues.zh: 更好的理解框架是你要做终局者。你要成为某个品类里的最后一家公司。这些才是真正有价值的企业。Microsoft 是最后的操作系统，至少几十年内都是如此。Google 是最后的搜索引擎。Facebook 只要最终被证明是最后一个社交网站，它就会极具价值。理解这种终局价值的一种视角是：这些公司绝大部分的价值都存在于遥远的未来。

cues.en: If you do sort of a discounted cash flow analysis of a business, you look at, you have sort of all these profit streams. You have a growth rate. The growth rate's much higher than the discount rate. And so most of the value exists far in the future. I did, I did this exercise at PayPal in March of 2001. We'd been in business for about 27 months. And and we sort of had, you know, the growth rate was 100% a year. We were discounting future cash flows by about 30%.
cues.zh: 如果你对一家企业做折现现金流分析，你会看所有这些利润流。你有一个增长率。增长率远高于折现率。所以大部分价值存在于遥远的未来。2001年3月，我在PayPal做过这个练习。当时我们已经经营了大约27个月。我们的增长率大约是每年100%。我们用大约30%的折现率来折现未来现金流。

cues.en: And it turned out that about three quarters of the value of the business as of 2001 came from cash flows in years 2011 and beyond. And whenever you do the math on any of these tech companies, you get to an answer that's something like that. So if you are trying to analyze any of the tech companies in Silicon Valley, Airbnb, Twitter, Facebook, any emerging Internet companies, all the ones in Y Combinator, the math tells you that.
cues.zh: 结果发现，2001年时这家企业约四分之三的价值来自2011年及以后的现金流。而只要你算任何这类科技公司，都会得到类似的结果。所以如果你想分析硅谷的任何科技公司，Airbnb、Twitter、Facebook，任何新兴互联网公司，所有Y Combinator里的公司，数学都会告诉你这一点。

cues.en: 3 quarters, 80, 85% of the value is coming from cash flows in years 2024 and beyond. It's very, very far in the future. And so one of the things that we always overvalue in Silicon Valley is growth rates, and we undervalue durability. Because growth is something you can measure in the here and now, and you can always track that very precisely. The question of whether a company's still going to be around a decade from now, that's actually would.
cues.zh: 四分之三，80%、85%的价值来自2024年及以后的现金流。那是非常非常遥远的未来。所以我们在硅谷总是高估的东西之一就是增长率，而低估了持久性。因为增长是当下就能衡量的东西，而且你总能非常精确地追踪它。而一家公司十年后是否还在，实际上才……

cues.en: what dominates the value equation and that sort of is a much more qualitative sort of a thing. And so if we went back to this idea of these characteristics of monopoly, proprietary technology, network effects, economies of scale, you can think of these characteristics as ones that exist at a moment in time where you capture a market and take it over. But you also want to think about
cues.zh: 是主导价值等式的东西，而且这更偏定性。所以如果我们回到垄断、专有技术、网络效应、规模经济这些特征的概念，你可以把这些特征看作是在某个时点存在的东西：你抓住一个市场并把它拿下。但你也要考虑

cues.en: Are these things going to last over time? And so there's a time dimension to all these characteristics. So network effects often have a great time element where as the network scales, the network effects actually get more robust. And so if you have a network effect business, that's often one that can become a bigger and stronger monopoly over time. Proprietary technology is always a little bit of a tricky one. So you want something that's ordered magnitude better than.
cues.zh: 这些东西能不能长期持续？所以所有这些特征都有时间维度。网络效应往往有很强的时间要素：随着网络扩大，网络效应实际上会变得更强。所以如果你有一家网络效应企业，它往往能随着时间变成更大、更强的垄断。专有技术总是有点棘手。所以你要的是比……好一个数量级的东西。

cues.en: the state of the art in the world today. And that's how you get people's attention. That's how you initially break through. But then you don't want to be superseded by somebody else. And so there are all these areas of innovation where there was tremendous innovation, but no one made any money. So describe manufacturing in the 1980s. You could build a better describe than anybody else. You could take over the whole world and
cues.zh: 当今世界最先进水平。这样你才能引起人们注意。这样你才能最初实现突破。但之后你不想被别人取代。所以有很多创新领域，出现了巨大的创新，却没人赚到钱。以20世纪80年代的磁盘驱动器制造业为例。你能造出比任何人都更好的磁盘驱动器。你能占领全世界，而

cues.en: Two years later, someone else would come along and replace yours. And in the course of 15 years, you got vastly improved disk drives. So it had great benefit to consumers, but it didn't actually help the people who started these companies. And so there's always this question about having a huge breakthrough in technology, but then also being able to say, explain why yours will be the last breakthrough.
cues.zh: 两年后，别人就会出现并取代你的产品。在15年里，磁盘驱动器得到了极大改进。所以这对消费者大有好处，但并没有真正帮到这些公司的创办者。所以问题始终是：你既要在技术上取得巨大突破，又得能够说明，为什么你的突破会是最后一次突破。

cues.en: or at least the last breakthrough for a long time. Or you make a breakthrough and then you can keep improving on it at a quick enough pace that no one can ever catch up. So if you have a structure of the future where there's a lot of innovation and other people will come up with new things in the thing you're working on, that's great for society. It's actually not that good for your business typically.
cues.zh: 或者至少是很长一段时间内的最后一次突破。又或者你取得突破后，能以足够快的步伐持续迭代，让别人永远追赶不上。所以，如果你构想的未来格局充满大量创新，别人也能在你做的领域里不断推陈出新，这对社会是天大的好事。但通常对你的商业来说并不算好。

cues.en: And then economies of scale, we already talked about. So, so I think, anyway, so I think this last mover thing is, is very critical. I'm always tempted, you know, I don't want to overdo the chess analogies, but, you know, the first mover in chess is someone who plays white. White is about a one-third of a pawn advantage. So there's a small advantage to going first. You want to be the last mover who, who wins the game. And so, so there's always the Capablanca world champion chess champion Capablanca line. You must begin by studying the end game.
cues.zh: 至于规模经济，我们之前已经讲过了。所以总之，我认为这种“后发者”思维极其关键。我总忍不住想打个比方，虽然我不想过度类比国际象棋，但象棋里的先发者就是执白棋的人。白棋大概有三分之一个兵的优势，先手确实有微弱优势。但你真正想做的是赢得终局的后发者。所以总能听到国际象棋世界冠军 Capablanca 的那句名言：你必须从研究残局开始。

cues.en: And I do think that's, I wouldn't say that's the only thing you should study. I think this sort of perspective of asking these questions, why will this still be the leading company 10, 15, 20 years from now, is a really critical one to try to think through. Let me sort of, I want to sort of go in two slightly other directions with this monopoly versus competition idea. And I think, so I think this is the,
cues.zh: 我觉得……倒不是说这是唯一该研究的，但我认为提出这种问题的视角——为什么这家公司在 10 年、15 年或 20 年后依然会是领头羊——是极其关键、必须想透彻的。关于垄断与竞争这个概念，我想稍微引向另外两个方向。我认为，这就是……

cues.en: The central idea in my mind for business, for starting business, for thinking about them. And there are some very interesting perspectives I think it gives on the whole history of innovation in technology and science. Because we've lived through 250, 300 years of incredible technological progress in many, many different domains. Steam engine to.
cues.zh: 我心中关于商业、关于创业以及思考商业的核心理念。而且我认为它为整个科技与科学创新史提供了一些非常有趣的视角。因为在过去的两三百年里，我们在许多不同领域见证了惊人的技术进步。从蒸汽机到……

cues.en: railways to telephones, refrigeration, household appliances, the computer revolution, aviation, all sorts of different areas of technological innovation. And then there's sort of analogous thing that one can say about science, where we've lived through centuries of enormous amounts of innovation in science as well. And the thing that I think people always miss when they-
cues.zh: 铁路、电话、制冷技术、家用电器、计算机革命、航空业，各类技术创新的不同领域。同样也可以这样看待科学，几个世纪以来我们在科学界也经历了海量的创新。而我认为人们在思考这些事情时往往忽略了一点，就是当他们……

cues.en: think about these things is that because x and y are independent variables, some of these things can be extremely valuable innovations. But the people who invent them, who come up with them, do not get rewarded for this. And certainly, if you go back to, you need to create x dollars in value, you capture y percent of x. I would suggest that the history of science has generally been one where y is 0%.
cues.zh: 思考这些事情时忽略了，因为 x 和 y 是两个独立变量，其中一些创新可能价值连城。但发明并提出它们的人，却没有因此得到回报。当然，如果回到公式：你创造了 x 美元的价值，然后捕获其中 y% 的价值。我认为整个科学史基本上就是一个 y 等于 0% 的历史。

cues.en: across the board, the scientists never make any money. They're always deluded into thinking that they live in a just universe that will reward them for their work and for their inventions. And this is probably the fundamental delusion that scientists tend to suffer from in our society. And even in technology, there are sort of many different areas of technology where there were great innovations that created tremendous value for society. But people did not
cues.zh: 放眼望去，科学家从没赚到过钱。他们总是有种错觉，以为自己生活在一个公平的宇宙里，世界会因为他们的付出和发明给予回报。这大概是科学家在我们社会中普遍存在的根本幻象。甚至在技术领域，也有很多领域涌现出伟大的创新，为社会创造了巨大的价值。但人们并没能……

cues.en: did not actually capture that much of the value. And so I think there is this sort of whole history of science and technology that can be told from the perspective of how much value was actually captured. And certainly there are entire sectors where people.
cues.zh: 实际上并没能捕获到那么多价值。所以我认为完全可以从“究竟捕获了多少价值”这个视角，来重新讲述整个科技史。当然，有些整个行业中，人们……

cues.en: didn't capture anything. So you're the smartest physicist of the 20th century. You come up with special relativity. You come up with general relativity. You don't get to be a billionaire. You don't even get to be a millionaire. It just somehow doesn't work that way. The railroads, incredibly valuable. Most of them just went bankrupt because it was too much competition. Wright Brothers, you fly the first plane, you don't make any money. And so I think there is sort of a structure to these industries that's very important.
cues.zh: 什么也没捕捉到。所以你是20世纪最聪明的物理学家。你提出了狭义相对论，提出了广义相对论，但你成不了亿万富翁，甚至成不了百万富翁。事情好像就不是这么运作的。铁路价值惊人，但大多数都破产了，因为竞争太激烈。莱特兄弟飞了第一架飞机，但没赚到钱。所以我认为这些行业存在一种结构，这非常重要。

cues.en: And I think the thing that's actually rare are the success cases. So it's actually, when you really think about the history in this 250 year sweep, Y is almost always 0%. It's always zero in science. It's almost always in technology. And so it's very rare where people made money.
cues.zh: 而我认为真正罕见的是成功案例。所以当你真正回顾这250年的历史时，Y几乎总是0%。在科学中总是零，在技术中也几乎总是如此。所以人们赚到钱的情况非常罕见。

cues.en: The late 18th, early 19th century, the first industrial revolution was the textile mills. You had the steam engine, you sort of automated things. And you had these relentless improvements that people improved efficiency of textile factories, of manufacturing generally, at a clip of five to seven percent every year, year after year, decade after decade. You had 60, 70 years of tremendous improvement from 1780 to 1850.
cues.zh: 18世纪末、19世纪初，第一次工业革命是纺织厂。有了蒸汽机，一些东西实现了自动化。然后是无休止的改进，人们提高纺织厂、乃至整个制造业的效率，速度是每年5%到7%，年复一年，十年又十年。从1780年到1850年，有60、70年的巨大进步。

cues.en: But even in 1850, most of the wealth in Britain was still held by the landed aristocracy. The workers didn't, you know, the workers didn't make that much. The capitalists didn't make that much either. It was all competed away. There were hundreds of people running textile factories. It was an industry that just the structure of the competition prevented people from, from making any money. And so I think there are, in my mind, there are probably are only
cues.zh: 但即使在1850年，英国的大部分财富仍掌握在地主贵族手中。工人没赚到多少钱，资本家也没赚到多少。全都被竞争掉了。有成百上千的人经营纺织厂。这个行业的竞争结构本身就让人赚不到钱。所以在我看来，过去这段历史里可能只有

cues.en: two broad categories in the entire history of the last 250 years where people have actually come up with new things and made money doing so. One is these sort of vertically integrated complex monopolies which people did build in the second industrial revolution at the end of the 19th and start of the 20th century. And so this was like Ford, it was the vertically integrated oil companies like Standard Oil.
cues.zh: 在过去250年的整个历史中，人们真正创造出新东西并因此赚钱的，大概只有两大类别。一类是垂直整合的复杂垄断企业，人们在19世纪末、20世纪初的第二次工业革命中建起了这类公司。比如福特，比如标准石油这样的垂直整合石油公司。

cues.en: And what these vertically integrated monopolies typically required was this very complex coordination. You got a lot of pieces to fit together in just the right way. When you assembled it, you had a tremendous advantage. This is actually done surprisingly little today. And so I think this is sort of a business form that when people can pull it off is very valuable. It's typically fairly capital intensive. We live sort of in a culture where it's very hard to get people.
cues.zh: 而这些垂直整合的垄断企业通常需要非常复杂的协调。你要把很多部分以恰到好处的方式拼在一起。当你组装起来时，就拥有巨大优势。今天真正这样做的人少得惊人。所以我认为这是一种商业模式，一旦有人能做成，就非常有价值。它通常相当资本密集。我们身处的文化，让人很难招到人。

cues.en: to buy into anything that's super complicated and takes very long to build. But when I sort of think about my colleague Elon Musk from PayPal success with Tesla and SpaceX, I think the key to these companies was the complex, vertically integrated monopoly structure they had. So if you sort of look at Tesla or SpaceX, if you ask, was there sort of a single breakthrough? I mean, they certainly innovated on a lot of dimensions. I don't think there was a single-
cues.zh: 去相信任何极其复杂、建设周期又很长的东西。但当我想到我在 PayPal 的同事 Elon Musk 在 Tesla 和 SpaceX 上的成功时，我觉得这些公司的关键在于它们那种复杂的、垂直整合的垄断结构。所以如果你看看 Tesla 或 SpaceX，问一句：是否存在某个单一突破？我是说，它们当然在很多维度上都创新了。我不认为存在某个单一的——

cues.en: 10x breakthrough in battery storage, or maybe working on some things on rocketry. But there was no sort of single massive breakthrough. But what was really impressive was integrating all these pieces together and doing it in a way that was more vertically integrated than most of their competitors. So Tesla, you also integrated the car distributors so they wouldn't steal all the money as.
cues.zh: 电池储能上的十倍级突破，或者也许在火箭技术的某些方面。但并没有某个单一的巨大突破。真正令人印象深刻的是，把所有部件整合在一起，并且以比大多数竞争对手更垂直整合的方式来做。Tesla 也是如此，你还整合了汽车经销商，免得它们把所有的钱都赚走，就像

cues.en: has happened with the rest of the car industry in the US. Or SpaceX, you basically pulled in all the subcontractors where most of the large aerospace companies have single source subcontractors that are able to sort of charge monopoly profits and make it very hard for the integrated aerospace companies to make money. And so vertical integration I think is sort of a.
cues.zh: 美国汽车业其他地方发生的那样。或者 SpaceX，你基本上把所有的分包商都收了进来，而大多数大型航空航天公司都有单一来源分包商，这些分包商能收取垄断利润，让垂直整合的航空航天公司很难赚钱。所以我认为垂直整合是一种

cues.en: a very underexplored modality of technological progress that people would do well to look at more. And then I think there is something about software itself that's very, very powerful. Software has these incredible economies of scale, these low marginal costs. And there is something about the world of bits as opposed to the world of atoms where you can often get very fast adoption. And the fast adoption is critical to-
cues.zh: 非常未被充分探索的技术进步模式，人们最好多关注一下。然后我觉得软件本身也有某种非常非常强大的东西。软件有惊人的规模经济、很低的边际成本。而且比特世界相对于原子世界，有个特点：你往往能实现非常快的采用。而快速采用对于

cues.en: capturing and taking over markets. Because even if you have a small market, if the adoption rate is too slow, there'll be enough time for other people to enter that market and compete with you. Whereas if you have a small to mid-sized market and have a fast adoption rate, you cannot take over this market. And so I think this is one of the reasons Silicon Valley has done so well and why software has been.
cues.zh: 占领并接管市场至关重要。因为即使市场很小，如果采用速度太慢，别人就有足够时间进入这个市场和你竞争。而如果你有一个中小型市场，并且采用速度很快，你就能接管这个市场。所以我认为这是硅谷做得如此出色的原因之一，也是软件成为

cues.en: of this phenomenal industry. And what I would suggest, what I want to leave you with is there are sort of these different rationalizations people give for why certain things work and why certain things don't work. And I think these rationalizations always obscure this question of creating x dollars in value and capturing y percent of x. So the science rationalization we're always told is that the scientists aren't interested in making money.
cues.zh: 这个非凡产业的原因之一。我想建议、想留给你们的是：人们会给出各种合理化说辞，解释某些东西为什么行得通、某些为什么行不通。而我认为这些说辞总是掩盖了这个问题：创造 x 美元价值，并捕获其中 y% 的 x。我们总被告知的科学界说辞是，科学家对赚钱不感兴趣。

cues.en: They're doing it for charitable reasons and that you're not a good scientist if you're motivated by money. And I'm not even saying people should always be motivated by money or something like this. But I think we should be a little bit more critical of this as a rationalization we should ask. Is this a rationalization to obscure the fact that Y equals 0% and the scientists are operating in this sort of world where all the innovation is effectively competed away and they can't capture.
cues.zh: 他们做这个是为了慈善原因，而且如果你被金钱驱动，你就不是个好科学家。我甚至不是说人们应该总是被金钱驱动之类。但我觉得我们应该对这种合理化说辞稍微更批判一点，应该问：这是不是一种说辞，用来掩盖 Y 等于 0%、科学家们处在这样一种世界里——所有创新实际上都被竞争消耗掉，而他们无法捕获价值？

cues.en: any of it directly. And then the software distortion that often happens is because people are making such vast fortunes in software, we infer that this is the most valuable thing in the world being done full stop. And so if people at Twitter make billions of dollars, it must be that Twitter is worth far more than anything Einstein did. And what that sort of rationalization tends to obscure
cues.zh: 并不能直接看懂其中任何一部分。接着，软件领域经常出现的扭曲是：人们在软件上赚了巨额财富，我们就推断这是世界上正在做的最有价值的事，仅此而已。于是如果 Twitter 的人赚了几十亿美元，那 Twitter 就一定比 Einstein 做过的任何事都值钱得多。而这种合理化往往会掩盖

cues.en: is again that X and Y are independent variables and there are these businesses where you capture a lot of X and there are others where you don't. And so I do think the history of innovation has been this history where the microeconomics, the structure of these industries has mattered a tremendous amount. And there is sort of this story where some people have made vast fortunes because they were in industries with the right structure and other people
cues.zh: 仍然是，X 和 Y 是独立变量；有些生意能让你捕获大量 X，另一些则不能。所以我确实认为，创新史一直是这样的历史：这些行业的微观经济学、行业结构极其重要。也有这样一种叙事：一些人赚得巨额财富，是因为身处结构合适的行业，而另一些人

cues.en: made nothing at all because they were in these sort of very competitive things. And we shouldn't just rationalize that way. I think it's worth understanding this better. And then finally, let me come back to this sort of overarching theme for this talk. This competition is for losers idea, which is always this provocative way to title things. Because we always think of the losers as the people who are not good at competing. We think of the losers as the people who are
cues.zh: 则一无所获，因为他们处在竞争极其激烈的那类行业。我们不该只这样合理化。我认为值得更好地理解这一点。最后，让我回到这次演讲的总体主题。“竞争是失败者的游戏”这个想法——这种标题总是很挑衅。因为我们总把失败者想成不擅长竞争的人。我们把失败者想成那些

cues.en: slow on the track team in high school or who do a little bit less well on the standardized tests and don't get into the right schools. And so we always think of losers as people who can't compete. And I want us to really rethink and revalue this and consider whether it's possible that competition itself is off, that we're sort of.
cues.zh: 在高中田径队里跑得慢的人，或标准化考试稍差、没进对学校的人。所以我们总把失败者想成不会竞争的人。我想让我们真正重新思考和重新评估这一点，想想有没有可能竞争本身就有问题，我们有点……

cues.en: It's not just the case that we don't understand this monopoly competition dichotomy intellectually. So I've just sort of been talking about why you wouldn't understand it intellectually, because people lie about it, it's distorted. We have all these, the history of innovation rationalizes what's happening in all these very, very strange ways. But I think it's more than just an intellectual blind spot. I think it's also a psychological blind spot where we.
cues.zh: 不只是我们在理智上不理解垄断与竞争这种二分法。我刚才在讲为什么你在理智上不会理解它，因为人们对此撒谎，它被扭曲了。创新史用各种非常非常奇怪的方式为正在发生的事合理化。但我认为这不仅是理智盲点。我认为它也是心理盲点，让我们

cues.en: find ourselves very, very attracted to competition in one form or another. We find it reassuring if other people do things. The word ape already in the time of Shakespeare meant both primate and imitate. And there is something about human nature that's deeply memetic, imitative, ape like, sheep like, lemming like, herd like. And it's this very, very problematic thing that we need to always think through and try to overcome. And there is always this question about
cues.zh: 发现自己非常非常容易被某种形式的竞争吸引。如果别人也在做某件事，我们会觉得安心。ape 这个词在莎士比亚时代就已既指灵长类，也指模仿。人性中有某种深层的东西：模因式、模仿式、类猿、从众、旅鼠式、羊群式。这是非常非常成问题的东西，我们需要始终想清楚并努力克服。而且总有一个问题：

cues.en: competition as a form of validation where we go for things that lots of other people are going for. And it's not that there is wisdom in crowds. It's not when lots of people are trying to do something that that's proof of it being valuable. I think it's when lots of people are trying to do something that is often proof of insanity. There are 20,000 people a year who move to Los Angeles to become movie stars. About 20 of them make it. I think the Olympics are a little bit better because you have
cues.zh: 把竞争当作一种认可，于是我们去追很多人都在追的东西。并不是说人多就有智慧。并不是很多人想做某事，就证明那事有价值。我认为，很多时候很多人想做某事，恰恰证明这很疯狂。每年有 2 万人搬到洛杉矶想当电影明星。大约 20 人成功。我觉得奥运会稍微好一点，因为你有

cues.en: You can sort of figure out pretty quickly whether you're good or not. So there's a little bit less of a dead weight loss to society. The sort of educational experience at a place, the pre-Stanford educational experience. There's always sort of a non-competitive characterization. I think most of the people in this room had machine guns. They were competing with people with bows and arrows. So it wasn't exactly a parallel competition when you were in junior high school and high school.
cues.zh: 你能很快判断自己是否擅长。所以对社会的无谓损失稍微少一点。某个地方的教育经历，斯坦福之前的教育经历。总有一种非竞争性的描述。我觉得这个房间里大多数人都有机关枪。他们是在和拿弓箭的人竞争。所以你在初中和高中时，那并不是完全对等的竞争。

cues.en: There's always a question, does the tournament make sense as you keep going? And so there is always this question, if people go on to grad school or post-doctoral educations, does the intensity of the competition really make sense? There's the classic Henry Kissinger line describing his fellow faculty at Harvard that the battles were so ferocious because the stakes were so small.
cues.zh: 大家总会问，一路这样卷下去真的有意义吗？所以总会有这样的疑问：如果继续读研或做博士后，如此激烈的竞争真的值得吗？Henry Kissinger 曾有一句名言来形容他在 Harvard 的教职同事：“竞争之所以如此残酷，正是因为筹码太小了。”

cues.en: describing sort of academia. And you sort of think on one level, this is a description of insanity. Why would people.
cues.zh: 用来形容学术界再贴切不过。在某种层面上你会觉得，这简直就是一种疯狂。为什么人们……

cues.en: fight like crazy when the stakes are so small. But it's also, I think, simply a function of the logic of the situation. When it's really hard to differentiate yourself from other people, when the objective differences really are small, then you have to compete ferociously to maintain a difference of one sort or another that's often more imaginary than real. There's always sort of a-
cues.zh: 会在筹码如此微不足道时拼得你死我活？但我认为，这其实只是局势逻辑的必然产物。当你很难让自己与众不同，当客观差距微乎其微时，你就不得不残酷竞争，去维持某种差异——而这种差异往往更多是想象出来的，并非真实存在。我常常会讲一个……

cues.en: a personal version of this that I tell where I was sort of hyper, hyper-tracked. My eighth grade junior high school yearbook, one of my friends wrote in, I know you'll get into Stanford in four years as a sophomore. I sort of went into Stanford four years later at the end of high school. Went to Stanford Law School. Ended up at a big law firm in New York where from the outside everybody wanted to get in. On the inside everybody wanted to leave.
cues.zh: 我亲身经历的故事：我曾经就是沿着既定轨道一路狂奔。初二的年鉴上，我一个朋友写道：“我知道你四年后高二就能进 Stanford。”四年后高中毕业，我确实进了 Stanford。之后又上了 Stanford 法学院。最终去了纽约一家大律所，外面的人挤破头想进去，里面的人拼了命想逃出来。

cues.en: And it was this very strange dynamic where after I sort of realized this was maybe not the best idea, and left after seven months and three days, one of the people down the hall from me told me, it's really reassuring to see you leave, Peter. I had no idea that it was possible to escape from Alcatraz, which of course, all you had to do was go out the front door and not come back. But so much of people's identities.
cues.zh: 那种氛围非常诡异，后来我意识到这可能不是什么好选择，在待了七个月零三天后离开了。走廊对面的一个同事对我说：“Peter，看到你离开真让人安心，我从没想过居然有人能逃出 Alcatraz 监狱。”但其实，你只需要走出大门，不再回头就行了。然而太多人的身份认同……

cues.en: got wrapped up in winning these competitions that they somehow lost sight of what was important, what was valuable. Competition does make you better at whatever it is that you're competing on. Because when you're competing, you're comparing yourself with the people around you. You're figuring out, how do I beat the people next to me? How do I do somewhat better at whatever it is they're doing? And you will get better at that thing. I'm not questioning that. I'm not denying that. But it often comes at this tremendous price.
cues.zh: 都深陷于赢下这些竞争之中，以至于忽略了什么才是重要、有价值的。竞争确实能让你在所比拼的事情上变得更强。因为在竞争时，你总在和身边的人比较，琢磨着怎么打败身边的人，怎么在他们做的事情上比他们稍微好一点。你在那件事上确实会越来越强，我并不否认这点。但这种提升往往伴随着巨大的代价——

cues.en: that you stop asking some bigger questions about what's truly important and truly valuable. And so I would, I would say that don't always go through the tiny little door that everyone's trying to rush through. Maybe go around the corner and go through the vast gate that no one's taking. Thank you very much. I guess it's time for, do you want to take a few questions or, sorry? Oh yes, people want to take, I'll take a few questions, so we have a few minutes time. Yeah, go ahead.
cues.zh: 你不再去思考更宏大的问题，不再去想什么才真正重要、真正有价值。所以我想说，别总是去挤那扇所有人都想硬挤进去的窄门。不妨拐个弯，去走那扇空无一人的宽广之门。非常感谢大家。我想接下来……是想提几个问题吗，抱歉？好的，大家想提问，那我来回答几个问题，我们还有几分钟时间。好的，请讲。

cues.en: Yeah, as you mentioned earlier, often we're not things and perfect competition often looks similar because the narratives people tell, or the narratives we tell ourselves. Do you have any ways to easily determine the difference when you're looking at an idea or evaluating your own idea? Well, I'd say the question I always try to focus on is what is the actual market? So not what's the narrative of the market, because you can always tell a fictional story about a market that's much bigger or much smaller, but what is the-
cues.zh: 是的，正如你刚才提到的，垄断和完全竞争通常看起来很像，因为这取决于人们对外宣扬的叙事，或是我们给自己编造的故事。当你审视一个点子或评估自己的想法时，有什么简单的方法来分辨它们吗？嗯，我想说的是，我始终关注的核心问题是：真正的市场到底是什么？不要看关于市场的宣传叙事，因为你总能编造出一个大得多或小得多的虚构故事，关键在于——

cues.en: What is the real objective market? So it's always, yeah, you always try to figure it out, and you realize people have incentives to powerfully distort these things. Yeah? So which of the aspects of monopolies that you mentioned when you said it's all for options like Google, Excel? Well, they have network effects with the ad network. They had proprietary technology that gave them the initial lead, because they had the page rank algorithm, which was.

cues.zh: 一帮在手机上做各种山寨支付系统的公司。比如 Square，比如 PayPal。它们只是读卡器形状不同而已，它们就是靠这个做差异化的。一个是三角形，一个是正方形。可能到了某个时候，这些跟风模仿者连新形状都用光了。但对于 Palantir 来说，我们一开始专注于情报界，这是一个很小的细分市场。我们拥有一项采用了截然不同方法的专有技术，

cues.en: where it was focused on the human computer synthesis rather than the substitution which I think is the dominant paradigm. cues.zh: 它专注于人机协同融合，而不是当时占据主导地位的“机器替代人”范式。所以在市场切入方式和专有技术上，我觉得有很多可以说的。好的，请讲。“我们有设计思维方法论，还有精益思维，用来通过不创造人们不需要的东西来降低风险。

cues.zh: 但年轻的创新者该如何获得灵感，去打造经久不衰的复杂系统呢？”你能重复一下这个问题吗？好的，问题是我如何看待精益创业、通过获取用户反馈进行迭代的思维，对比那些可能行不通的复杂系统。我个人对所有的精益创业方法论都持相当怀疑的态度。我认为真正伟大的公司所做的事情，往往更像是一种跨越式的质的提升。

cues.en: that really differentiated them from everybody else. They typically did not do massive customer surveys. cues.zh: 这才是他们真正区别于其他人的地方。他们通常不做大规模客户调研。这些公司的经营者有时（并非总是）患有严重形式的阿斯伯格综合征，所以他们其实不太受他人想法或他人指令的影响，也不那么容易被打退。所以我确实认为，我们太专注于把迭代当作一种方式，而太少去尝试拥有，

cues.zh: 与公众之间一条虚拟的 ESP 链接，并自己去把它搞清楚。我会说，让我想想，我会说，这个，我不太确定，风险问题我觉得总是很棘手，因为存在……你知道，这不是……常常……我觉得常常是，你没有足够时间去真正降低风险。如果你要花足够时间搞清楚人们想要什么，往往到那时就已经错过机会了。

cues.en: And then of course there's always the risk of doing something that's not that significant or meaningful. So you could say a track in law school is a low risk track from one perspective. It may still be a very high risk track in the sense that maybe you have a high risk of not doing something meaningful with your life. So we have to think about risk in these very complicated way. I think risk is for this very complicated concept. Yes?
cues.zh: 当然，还总有做某件不那么重要或没那么有意义的事的风险。所以你可以说，从某个角度看，法学院的一条路径是低风险路径。它可能仍是一条非常高风险的路，因为也许你有很高风险，一生都没做什么有意义的事。所以我们得用这种非常复杂的方式思考风险。我觉得风险就是这么一个非常复杂的概念。对吧？

cues.en: In effect, they really were a big first mover in some sense. You could say Google was not the first search engine. There were other search engines before. Facebook was not the first social networking site. My friend Reed Hoffman started one in 1997. They called it SocialNet, so they already had the name social networking.
cues.zh: 实际上，他们在某种意义上确实是很重要的先行者。你可以说 Google 不是第一个搜索引擎。之前还有其他搜索引擎。但在一个维度上，他们比所有人都好得多。所以他们是第一个拥有 PageRank、采用某种自动化方法的。Facebook 不是第一个社交网站。我的朋友 Reed Hoffman 在 1997 年创办了一个。他们叫它 SocialNet，所以他们已经有 social networking 这个名字了，

cues.en: in the name of their company seven years before Facebook. Their idea was that it was gonna be this virtual cyberspace where I'd be a dog and you'd be a cat and we'd have all these different rules about how we'd interact with each other in this virtual alternate reality. Facebook was the first one to get real identity. So I'd say, I hope Facebook would be the last social networking site. It was the first one in a very important dimension. People often would not think of it as the first because they'd sort of lump all these things together. Okay, one more question. Let's take one here.
cues.zh: 在他们公司名称里，比 Facebook 早了七年。他们的想法是，这会是一个虚拟网络空间，我在里面当狗，你当猫，我们有一套套不同的规则，规定在这个虚拟平行现实中如何互动。Facebook 是第一个抓住真实身份的。所以我会说，我希望 Facebook 会是最后一个社交网站。它在一个非常重要的维度上是第一个。人们常常不把它看作第一个，因为他们会把这些东西混为一谈。好，再问一个问题。这里选一个。

cues.en: If you're theoretically someone who worked at Goldman Sachs out of college and left out at six months and is now studying computer science at Stanford, how would you recommend rethinking sort of that repetitive thing? cues.zh: 假设你大学毕业后去了 Goldman Sachs，干了六个月就离职，现在又在 Stanford 读计算机科学，你会建议如何反思这种重复陷入的怪圈？你看，我其实不太擅长，我不太懂心理咨询那套，所以我不太知道该怎么……

cues.en: I don't quite know how to solve this. There are these very odd studies they've done on people who go to business school. There's one they've done at Harvard Business School, where it's sort of the anti Asperger personality, where you have people who are super extroverted, generally have low convictions, a few ideas. And you have sort of a hot house environment. You put all these people in for two years.
cues.zh: 我不太清楚该怎么解决这个问题。有人对读商学院的人做过一些非常奇特的研究。其中一项是在哈佛商学院做的，那里的人可以说是典型的“反阿斯伯格人格”：极度外向，通常没什么坚定信念，也没什么独立想法。你把这些人放到一个像温室一样的环境里，关上两年。

cues.en: And at the end of it, they systematically end up, the largest cohort systematically ends up doing the wrong thing. They try to catch the last wave. In 1989, everyone at Harvard tried to work for Mike Milken. It was one or two years before he went to jail for all the junk bond stuff. They were never interested in Silicon Valley or tech except for 99, 2000 when they timed the dot com bubble peaking perfectly. And then 05 to 07 was housing, private equity stuff like this. So I do think this,
cues.zh: 到头来，他们绝大多数人总是会系统性地做出错误的选择。他们总想去赶最后一班车。1989年，哈佛的人人争着去为 Mike Milken 工作，而一两年后他就因垃圾债券丑闻入狱了。他们对硅谷或科技从来不感兴趣，除了在1999和2000年，极其精准地赶上了互联网泡沫的最顶峰。接着在2005到2007年，又是房地产、私募股权这类东西。所以我确实认为这种……

cues.en: tendency for us to see competition as validation is very deep. I don't think there's any sort of easy psychological formula to avoid it, so I don't quite know what sort of therapy to recommend. But my first starting point, which is only maybe 10% of the way, is to never underestimate how big a problem it is. We always think this is something that afflicts other people.
cues.zh: 把竞争视为自我价值证明的倾向是根深蒂固的。我觉得没有什么简单的心理技巧可以避开它，所以我也不知道该推荐什么样的心理疗法。但我的第一步建议——虽然这可能也只能解决 10% 的问题——就是绝不要低估这个问题的严重性。我们总以为受这困扰的都是别人。

cues.en: So it's easy for me to point to people in business schools or people at Harvard or people on Wall Street. I think it actually does afflict all of us to a very profound degree. We always think of advertising as things that work on other people. How, who are all these stupid people who fall for all those ads on TV? They obviously work to some extent, and they work to a disturbing extent on all of us. And it's something we, we all should work to overcome. Thank you very much.
cues.zh: 所以我很容易对商学院的人、哈佛的人或华尔街的人指指点点。但我认为它其实深深地影响着我们每一个人。我们总觉得广告只对别人管用：电视上那些广告，到底是什么傻子才会信啊？但它们显然在某种程度上奏效了，而且对我们所有人的影响大得令人不安。这是我们所有人都应该努力去克服的。非常感谢大家。
